input_cases.grading_notes: The three failure modes: (1) models mistakenly classify counterfeits as correct; (2) models are worse at reasoning about the execution behaviour of counterfeits and often predict their execution results as if they were correct; (3) when asked to fix counterfeits, the likelihood of successfully repairing a counterfeit is often even lower than that of sampling a correct program from scratch. A counterfeit is a program sampled from a language model that (1) has high enough log-probability to be generated at a moderate temperature and (2) passes weak correctness checks (e.g., compiling). The paper recommends caution when relying on models to understand their own samples, especially without external feedback.
input_cases.question: In 'The Counterfeit Conundrum: Can Code Language Models Grasp the Nuances of Their Incorrect Generations?' (Gu et al., ACL 2024), what are the three failure modes showing that models have a shallow understanding of counterfeit programs?

In sketching, the programmer writes a partial program (a sketch) with holes encoding the solution structure, and an automated synthesizer fills the low-level details to satisfy a reference implementation or a set of test routines.

input_cases.grading_notes: VLMaterial (Li et al., ICLR 2025) generates procedural materials—represented as functional node graphs—from an input image, a task that normally requires professional knowledge and significant effort. Core approach: convert procedural materials into standard Python programs and fine-tune a large pre-trained vision-language model (VLM) to generate such programs from input images. It also contributes an open-source procedural material dataset and performs program-level augmentation by prompting another pre-trained LLM. Acceptable quote: 'we leverage the ability to convert procedural materials into standard Python programs and fine-tune a large pre-trained vision-language model (VLM) to generate such programs from input images.' The method outperforms previous methods on both synthetic and real-world examples.

input_cases.grading_notes: StatusQuo (Cheung, Arden, Madden, Solar-Lezama, Myers; CIDR 2013) targets the strong separation between the application and database layers that makes end-to-end goals (performance, reliability, security) hard to satisfy. It uses program analysis and program synthesis to enable seamless movement of functionality between the database and application layers: it takes functionality originally written as imperative code and translates it into relational queries that execute in the database, and it makes runtime decisions about the optimal placement of computation to reduce data movement between the database and application server. It also adaptively alters the placement of code and data in response to environment changes such as machine load.
input_cases.question: How does the StatusQuo system aim to address end-to-end goals such as performance, reliability, and security?

input_cases.grading_notes: StatusQuo (Cheung et al., CIDR 2013). Note: the question deliberately paraphrases ('placement of computation') to test semantic/hybrid retrieval rather than exact keyword match.

input_cases.grading_notes: LINC = Logical Inference via Neurosymbolic Computation (Olausson, Gu, Lipkin, Zhang et al., EMNLP 2023). It reformulates logical reasoning as modular neurosymbolic programming: the LLM acts as a semantic parser that translates premises and conclusions from natural language into first-order logic, and those expressions are offloaded to an external theorem prover that performs deductive inference symbolically. Result: augmenting the comparatively small open-source StarCoder+ (15.5B parameters) with LINC outperforms GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting by an absolute 38% and 10%, respectively, on ProofWriter. With GPT-4, LINC scores 26% higher than CoT on ProofWriter while performing comparably on FOLIO. Evaluation datasets: FOLIO and a balanced subset of ProofWriter.
input_cases.question: What is LINC, and what result does it report on ProofWriter when augmenting StarCoder+?

input_cases.grading_notes: Nye, Pu, Bowers, Andreas, Tenenbaum, Solar-Lezama (ICLR 2021). Key challenge: representing the behavior of a partially written program before it can be executed, in order to judge whether it is on the right track and predict where to search next during program synthesis. Approach: inspired by abstract interpretation, they learn an approximate execution model implemented as a modular neural network, building compositional program representations. Partial programs are represented with a flexible combination of concrete execution state and learned neural representations, using the learned ('blended') approximate semantics where concrete semantics are unknown (unfinished parts). Result: these hybrid neuro-symbolic representations let execution-guided synthesizers use more powerful constructs such as loops and higher-order functions, and synthesize programs more accurately for a given search budget than pure neural approaches.
input_cases.question: In 'Representing Partial Programs with Blended Abstract Semantics', what is the key challenge and how do the authors address it?

input_cases.grading_notes: Ellis, Ritchie, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum (NeurIPS 2018). It learns to convert simple hand drawings into graphics programs written in a subset of LaTeX, combining deep learning and program synthesis. Two steps: (1) a convolutional neural network proposes plausible drawing primitives (e.g., rectangles, lines, circles) that explain the image—these primitives form a specification (spec) of what the program must draw; (2) a model uses program synthesis techniques to recover a graphics program from that spec. The programs include constructs like variable bindings, iterative loops, and simple conditionals. With the program recovered, they can correct errors made by the deep network and extrapolate drawings.
input_cases.question: What does 'Learning to Infer Graphics Programs from Hand-Drawn Images' do, and what two-step process does it use?

input_cases.grading_notes: Bastani, Pu, Solar-Lezama (NeurIPS 2018). VIPER is an algorithm that combines ideas from model compression and imitation learning to learn decision tree policies guided by a DNN policy (the 'oracle') and its Q-function. The goal is verifiable RL: decision tree policies are nonparametric (can represent complex policies) yet highly structured (efficiently verifiable). Demonstrations: (i) a provably robust decision tree policy for a variant of Atari Pong with a symbolic state space; (ii) a policy for a toy Pong-based game that provably never loses; (iii) a provably stable policy for cart-pole. In each case the decision tree policy matches the performance of the original DNN policy.
input_cases.question: What is VIPER in 'Verifiable Reinforcement Learning via Policy Extraction', and what does it produce?

input_cases.grading_notes: Pu, Miranda, Solar-Lezama, Kaelbling (ICML 2018). Program synthesis is framed as a constraint satisfaction problem where input-output examples are encoded as constraints and solved with a constraint solver; the key challenge is scalability, since a large set of examples incurs significant time and memory overhead. The method discovers a subset of examples that is both small and representative: the subset is built iteratively, using a neural network to predict the probability of unchosen examples conditioned on the already-chosen ones, and greedily adding the least probable example. Empirically, such subsets significantly improve synthesis time and stability. (The paper references CEGIS—counterexample-guided inductive synthesis—as the standard baseline.)
input_cases.question: What method does 'Selecting Representative Examples for Program Synthesis' propose, and why is it needed?

(Blended Abstract Semantics, ICLR 2021) frame inductive synthesis as search over a vast combinatorial space of programs from examples, emphasizing the challenge of representing partial-program behavior to guide the search. Evidence: (1) using a stronger model to artificially boost the quality of the feedback yields substantially larger performance gains; (2) a small-scale study providing GPT-4 with feedback from human participants shows that even for the strongest models, self-repair still lags far behind what can be achieved with human-level debugging.

Models studied: Code Llama, GPT-3.5, GPT-4; benchmarks: HumanEval and APPS.

input_cases.grading_notes: Ellis, Morales, Sablé-Meyer, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum (NeurIPS 2018). Successful program induction usually requires a hand-engineered domain-specific language (DSL). EC2 is a program induction algorithm that learns a DSL while jointly training a neural network to efficiently search for programs in the learned DSL. In other words, it learns a domain-specific library of reusable program components at the same time as it learns to search. It was used to synthesize functions on lists, edit text, and solve symbolic regression problems.
input_cases.question: What is the EC2 algorithm in 'Library Learning for Neurally-Guided Bayesian Program Induction', and what does it learn?

input_cases.grading_notes: Three domains: synthesizing functions on lists (list functions), editing text (text editing), and solving symbolic regression problems. In each domain the model learns a domain-specific library of program components for expressing solutions. The paper connects to practical program-induction systems such as FlashFill (embedded in Excel).
input_cases.question: On which domains do the authors of 'Library Learning for Neurally-Guided Bayesian Program Induction' demonstrate EC2?

input_cases.grading_notes: It presents a method for synthesizing recursive functions that provably satisfy a given specification expressed as a polymorphic refinement type. At the core is a new algorithm for refinement type checking that supports specification decomposition. (This system is known as Synquid.) The programmer provides a refinement-type signature, and the synthesizer produces a program guaranteed to meet it.
input_cases.question: What does 'Program Synthesis from Polymorphic Refinement Types' (Polikarpova, Kuraj, Solar-Lezama; PLDI 2016) synthesize, and from what kind of specification?

input_cases.grading_notes: Two reasons: (1) polymorphic refinement types offer a unique combination of expressive power and decidability, which enables automatic verification—and hence synthesis—of nontrivial programs; (2) a type-based specification can often be effectively decomposed into independent specifications for its components, so the synthesizer considers fewer component combinations, giving a combinatorial reduction in the size of the search space. The key to scalable synthesis is modular verification.
input_cases.question: Why do the authors of 'Program Synthesis from Polymorphic Refinement Types' argue refinement types are especially well suited to program synthesis?

input_cases.grading_notes: Evaluated on a large set of synthesis problems, the prototype exceeded the state of the art in both scalability and usability. It synthesized more complex programs than prior work—e.g., several sorting algorithms and operations on balanced search trees—as well as most benchmarks tackled by existing synthesizers, often starting from more concise and intuitive user input.

It reports an accuracy of 79.53%, which approaches human performance (80%), outperforming multiple baseline methods.

input_cases.grading_notes: The goal is to build systems that write code automatically from specifications humans can easily provide, such as examples and natural language. The key idea is that a flexible combination of pattern recognition and explicit reasoning can solve complex programming problems. The novel intermediate representation (program sketches—schematic outlines of full programs with holes) and training algorithm let a synthesis system learn, without direct supervision, when to rely on pattern recognition (neural) and when to perform symbolic search.

The intermediate program-sketch representation is what allows it to dynamically integrate the two types of information.

input_cases.grading_notes: LiveCodeBench is a comprehensive, contamination-free evaluation of LLMs for code. It continuously collects new problems over time from contests across three competition platforms: LeetCode, AtCoder, and Codeforces. It was motivated by the observation that existing benchmarks (e.g., HumanEval, MBPP) suffer from data contamination, overfitting, saturation, and a narrow focus on code generation.
input_cases.question: What is LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., ICLR 2025) and which platforms does it draw problems from?

input_cases.grading_notes: LiveCodeBench evaluates a broader range of code-related capabilities such as self-repair, code execution, and test output prediction, beyond just code generation. It hosts over six hundred coding problems published between May 2023 and August 2024, and the authors evaluate over 50 LLMs—the largest evaluation study of code LLMs on competition problems.
input_cases.question: Beyond code generation, what capabilities does LiveCodeBench evaluate, and how large is it?

input_cases.grading_notes: By using time-segmented evaluations: because each problem is tagged with a release date, models can be evaluated only on problems published after their training cutoff date. The authors show a stark performance drop for models (e.g., DeepSeek, GPT-4-O, Claude) on problems released after their cutoff, revealing contamination; evaluating only on post-cutoff time windows is a robust way to evade it.
input_cases.question: How does LiveCodeBench detect and avoid data contamination?

input_cases.grading_notes: It introduces an unsupervised learning algorithm that combines probabilistic modeling with solver-based techniques for program synthesis, learning programs from noisy observations without explicit input/output examples. Domains: a visual learning domain (learning many visual concepts from only a few examples) and a language learning problem (recovering some English inflectional morphology). It gives a new approach to unsupervised learning of symbolic compositional structures and a technique for applying program synthesis tools to noisy data.
input_cases.question: What does 'Unsupervised Learning by Program Synthesis' (Ellis, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum; NeurIPS 2015) propose, and on what domains is it evaluated?

input_cases.grading_notes: Deep RL policies typically struggle to generalize to novel environments. The paper proposes learning programmatic state machine policies that capture repeating behaviors, giving them the ability to generalize to instances requiring an arbitrary number of repetitions—a property the authors call inductive generalization. State machine policies mix continuous and discrete structure, making them hard to learn. Traditional neural network policies fail to inductively generalize on these tasks.
input_cases.question: What problem does 'Synthesizing Programmatic Policies that Inductively Generalize' (Inala et al., ICLR 2020) address, and what representation does it use?

input_cases.grading_notes: Adaptive teaching is the learning framework the paper proposes for learning a state machine policy by imitating a teacher. Unlike traditional imitation learning, the teacher adaptively updates itself based on the structure of the student (the programmatic state machine being learned). This lets the algorithm learn policies that inductively generalize to novel environments where traditional neural network policies do not.
input_cases.question: What is 'adaptive teaching' in 'Synthesizing Programmatic Policies that Inductively Generalize'?

input_cases.grading_notes: ENCOMPASS: Enhancing Agent Programming with Search Over Program Execution Paths (Li, Solar-Lezama, Yue, Zheng). Current approaches to agent programming often entangle two aspects of agent design: the core workflow logic and the inference-time strategy (e.g., tree search). PAN is a programming model that disentangles these two concerns, letting the programmer describe the agent workflow and independently experiment with different inference-time strategies by simply changing a few inputs.
input_cases.question: What is probabilistic angelic nondeterminism (PAN) in the ENCOMPASS paper (Li et al.), and what does it disentangle?

input_cases.grading_notes: ENCOMPASS provides an implementation of PAN in Python: it uses a Python decorator to compile agent workflow programs into a search space. The authors present three case studies showing how the framework lets a programmer quickly improve the reliability of an agent and easily switch between different inference-time strategies (such as best-of-N sampling, refinement, and tree search) with little additional coding. It is meant to be used alongside (not replace) prompting/tool-use frameworks like LangChain or DSPy.
input_cases.question: How is PAN implemented in the ENCOMPASS framework, and what did the authors demonstrate?

Do not replace this with the next sentence about Phind or with an invented caution about contamination. Normalize line breaks only.
input_cases.question: In CRUXEval's Appendix A, 'Limitations and Future Work', quote the complete sentence beginning 'One must' about using benchmarks to compare models.

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: precise_quote. Verbatim: “We show theoretically and empirically that RL performance gain from skills is worse in environments where solutions to states are less compressible.” Evidence: abstract, PDF page 1. Preserve 'worse' and 'less compressible'; reversing either changes the result. Normalize whitespace and line wrapping only. DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2406-07897.pdf is an acceptable version for this sentence.

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: boundary. No: SPARLING's sparse objects are local latent intermediate activations or motifs in an end-to-end concept-learning model, not document term vectors, a retrieval index, or BM25 ranking scores. Its abstract discusses motif identifiability under assumptions and a sparsity-enforcing informational bottleneck, with empirical intermediate-state localization. It does not supply a RAG retrieval-precision benchmark. Explicitly distinguish activation sparsity from sparse retrieval; do not invent a BM25 improvement. Evidence: abstract, PDF page 1, and Introduction, PDF page 2. DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2302-01976.pdf is an acceptable duplicate.
input_cases.question: SPARLING uses extreme sparsity. Does that make it evidence for improved sparse-document retrieval or BM25 ranking in a RAG system? Explain the object that is sparse in the actual paper.

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: multi_hop; hops: 2. Required dependency: Counterfeit Conundrum's repair-prompt attribution -> Olausson et al.'s Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? -> that paper's human-feedback results. Gold: The cited study is Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? (Olausson, Inala, Wang, Gao, Solar-Lezama, ICLR 2024). Table 1 reports overall repair success of 33.30% with GPT-4 feedback and 52.60% with human feedback, an increase of 19.30 percentage points (about 1.58 times). Section 4.3 recruited 16 participants, used 40 failing GPT-4 programs, collected two human feedback strings per program, and sampled 25 GPT-4 repairs per feedback/program pair; it also evaluated two GPT-4 feedback strings per program. These are conditional repair-success rates, not end-to-end benchmark pass rates or proportions of participants. The study explicitly did not measure the extra cognitive burden of keeping humans in the loop, so it does not establish a direct cost-benefit superiority of human-in-the-loop deployment. Evidence: DBLP_conf_acl_GuLJOLSS24.pdf PDF p.18, Appendix B.2 Repair and B.3 (printed p.91), plus reference entry PDF p.11 (printed p.84); DBLP_conf_iclr_OlaussonIW0S24.pdf PDF p.8, Section 4.3 and Table 1. Require both the attribution and the downstream experiment, not two unrelated summaries.
input_cases.question: The Counterfeit Conundrum says it adapted its repair prompt from an earlier study. Identify that study, then use its human-feedback experiment to report GPT-4's overall repair success with its own explanations versus human explanations. What was the size of that experiment, and why is this not a direct cost-benefit comparison of autonomous and human-assisted repair?

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: multi_hop; hops: 3. Required dependency: 2025 position paper's Jain et al. (2024b) citation -> LiveCodeBench -> its explicitly named code-execution inspiration CRUXEval -> CRUXEval construction. Gold: Jain et al. (2024b) is LiveCodeBench: Holistic and Contamination Free Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code. LiveCodeBench's Section 6.1, Code Execution paragraph, explicitly says its execution scenario is particularly inspired by CRUXEval. CRUXEval uses Code Llama 34B to generate a large pool of Python functions and inputs, executes the functions on the inputs to obtain outputs, filters for short programs with low computation and memory requirements/no complex arithmetic, and randomly selects 800 surviving functions. The benchmark's functions are 3–13 lines. Each has an input-output pair and supports input prediction (CRUXEval-I) and output prediction (CRUXEval-O). Do not say these are LiveCodeBench's human-submitted contest solutions: its paper explicitly contrasts its live, more complex, human-produced functions with CRUXEval. Evidence: DBLP_conf_icml_GuJLSESS25.pdf PDF p.6 Section 3.4 Contamination and p.15 Jain et al. 2024b reference; DBLP_conf_iclr_JainHGLYZWSSS25.pdf PDF p.10 Section 6.1 Code Execution; DBLP_conf_icml_GuRLSS024.pdf PDF p.1 Abstract and Section 1, p.2 construction paragraph (equivalent original construction in DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2401-03065.pdf pp.1–2 is an acceptable final-hop alias).
input_cases.question: In Position: Future Research and Challenges Remain Towards AI for Software Engineering, follow the Jain et al. (2024b) reference cited under Contamination. In that benchmark's paper, follow the benchmark named as the particular inspiration for its code-execution scenario. For this final benchmark, which model generated the candidate functions and inputs, how were outputs obtained, how many functions were retained, and what length and difficulty restrictions applied? Show the intermediate identities rather than jumping straight to the final facts.

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: multi_hop; hops: 4. Required dependency: MathDSL identifies Stitch -> Stitch identifies its DreamCoder deductive baseline -> DreamCoder explicitly credits EC2 -> EC2's original paper supplies stage definitions and training sources. Gold chain: MathDSL -> Stitch (Top-Down Synthesis for Library Learning) -> DreamCoder (Growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning) -> EC2/ECC (Library Learning for Neurally-Guided Bayesian Program Induction). EC2 expands to Explore/Compress/Compile. Explore searches for compact programs solving tasks using the current DSL and neural recognition model. Compress grows the DSL/library by finding reusable common fragments/regularities in discovered programs. Compile trains the recognition network to guide future program search, amortizing inference; the learned DSL represents the prior, and the network produces task-conditioned guidance. Its recognition model trains on both (1) real task/program pairs discovered by Explore and (2) synthetic fantasies: programs sampled from the current DSL and run to create input-output tasks. The first source has task-relevant quality; the second supplies unlimited synthetic data. Do not describe the recognition model as trained exclusively on externally labeled correct programs, and do not omit the intermediate identities. Evidence: DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2409-17490.pdf PDF p.2 Section 2; DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23.pdf PDF pp.1–2 Abstract/Introduction (explicit DreamCoder comparison, including Ellis et al. 2020); DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2006-08381.pdf PDF p.4 Introduction (explicit EC2 predecessor credit); DBLP_conf_nips_EllisMSST18.pdf PDF p.2 stage summary and pp.4–5 Section 2.3 training details. Hop count denotes four dependent source retrievals, not four pairwise comparisons or independent questions.
input_cases.question: Trace this library-learning lineage through the papers: start with the separate library learner used by MathDSL; in that learner's paper identify the wake-sleep system whose deductive library learner it evaluates against; in the wake-sleep system's paper identify the predecessor credited with first combining library learning and neurally guided program synthesis. Finally, in that predecessor's original paper, expand its acronym, explain its three stages, and state the two sources of training data for its recognition model. Give the complete chain with citations.

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: contradiction. Subtype: genuine version/snapshot update, not mutually exclusive empirical findings. Gold: The local arXiv v2 dated 6 June 2024 says over five hundred coding problems published between May 2023 and May 2024, and evaluates 18 base plus 34 instruction-tuned models. The ICLR 2025 paper says over six hundred coding problems published between May 2023 and August 2024, and evaluates over 50 LLMs. The benchmark deliberately collects new problems over time from LeetCode, AtCoder and CodeForces, so the different count/window pairs describe evolving snapshots. Do not claim exactly 500 or exactly 600, do not infer an exact addition of 100, and do not infer that the later model pool necessarily grew from 52 from its imprecise over-50 description. The correct resolution is version-aware reporting, not averaging counts or choosing a supposedly erroneous paper. Evidence: DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2403-07974.pdf PDF p.1 Abstract/date footer and p.2 live-update principle; DBLP_conf_iclr_JainHGLYZWSSS25.pdf PDF p.1 Abstract and p.2 live-update principle. These canonical files are different versions of the same work, not independent studies. The later appendix contains other scenario/window-specific counts; they must not be substituted for the explicitly requested headline snapshot.
input_cases.question: Two local versions of LiveCodeBench give different headline dataset sizes and collection end dates. Compare the June 2024 arXiv version with the ICLR 2025 version: what does each abstract say, and is this a contradiction about a fixed dataset or a documented update? Keep the date windows attached to the counts rather than combining them into one timeless total.

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: contradiction. Subtype: controlled apparent disagreement with explicit scope reconciliation; neither paper makes a universal opposite claim. Gold: Counterfeit Conundrum Section 3.3 deliberately withholds execution details: the model is only told the program did not pass, receives the original specification, and must explain/fix the counterfeit without a failing-test signal. Its per-problem mean repair success is compared with baseline unconditional pass@1, since drawing a new sample is an alternative repair strategy. Most plotted settings/problems fall below resampling, but the paper does not claim all repair is useless and acknowledges exceptions (e.g. 35/81 HumanEval problems for DeepSeek-33B exceed baseline). Silver Bullet's repair pipeline includes execution/error feedback from unit-test checking plus textual explanations, and it separates code and feedback models in some experiments. It compares repair with i.i.d. generation while accounting for sampling budgets, finding often modest, heterogeneous or absent gains; stronger model feedback and human feedback can improve repair substantially. Its human study raises overall conditional GPT-4 repair success from 33.30% to 52.60%, but does not measure the human cognitive cost. Appendix A also discusses token-cost-aware pass@t rather than assuming all sampled artifacts cost the same. Counterfeit Conundrum itself explicitly acknowledges prior success with failed-unit-test information and narrows its conclusion especially to settings without external feedback. Thus the papers support feedback quality and evaluation budget as important conditions, not opposite universal laws. They use different models/tasks and conditional samples as well, so their percentages cannot be ranked as a controlled head-to-head result. Evidence: DBLP_conf_acl_GuLJOLSS24.pdf PDF p.4 Section 3.3 (printed p.77) and p.18 Appendix B.2; DBLP_conf_iclr_OlaussonIW0S24.pdf PDF p.1 Abstract, pp.2–4 pipeline/Section 3, pp.5–8 Section 4 (especially Sections 4.2–4.3/Table 1), pp.13–14 Appendix A. Full credit requires stating that the apparent conflict dissolves under the stated scopes; a generic different tasks explanation without the concrete feedback/baseline distinction is insufficient.
input_cases.question: The Counterfeit Conundrum reports that repairing incorrect generations often loses to sampling anew, while Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? reports gains in some settings and substantially better repair with stronger feedback. Are these findings genuinely inconsistent? Reconcile them using the feedback each experiment supplies, the comparison baseline, and the cost qualifications; do not answer simply that one paper is newer.

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: enumeration; expected_unique_works: 11. Require all eleven works, not a sample. Gold list: (1) sk_p: a neural program corrector for MOOCs — seq2seq statement completion supplies candidate repairs, DBLP_conf_oopsla_PuNSB16.pdf (identical alias DBLP_journals_corr_PuNSB16.pdf), PDF p.1 and sections 2, 4. (2) Library Learning for Neurally-Guided Bayesian Program Induction (EC2) — trained recognition network guides search in the learned DSL, DBLP_conf_nips_EllisMSST18.pdf, PDF p.1 and section 2.3. (3) Learning to Infer Graphics Programs from Hand-Drawn Images — trained CNN proposes drawing specifications for subsequent program synthesis, DBLP_conf_nips_EllisRST18.pdf (version alias DBLP_journals_corr_EllisRST17.pdf), PDF p.1 and sections 2–3. (4) Learning to Infer Program Sketches (SketchAdapt) — trained sketch generator plus learned recognizer and symbolic enumeration, DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19.pdf (version alias DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1902-06349.pdf), PDF p.1 and sections 3–4. (5) Write, Execute, Assess: Program Synthesis with a REPL — trained policy/value models guide execution-state search, DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1906-04604.pdf, PDF p.1 and section 3.2. (6) Learning Compositional Rules via Neural Program Synthesis — neural rule-system proposals followed by symbolic checking, DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2003-05562.pdf, PDF p.1 and section 3. (7) DreamCoder: Growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning — learned neural recognition model guides program search while library abstractions grow, DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2006-08381.pdf, PDF p.1 and wake/sleep algorithm description. (8) Representing Partial Programs with Blended Abstract Semantics — learned modular neural semantics combined with concrete execution for synthesis search, DBLP_conf_iclr_NyePBATS21.pdf, PDF p.1 and section 3. (9) Fusion 360 Gallery: A Dataset and Environment for Programmatic CAD Construction from Human Design Sequences — includes its own trained neural policy and search for CAD construction sequences, not merely a dataset, DBLP_journals_tog_WillisPLCDLSM21.pdf, PDF p.1 and section 5.3. (10) MathDSL: A Domain-Specific Language for Concise Mathematical Solutions Via Program Synthesis — trains DreamCoder's neural search model for equation-solving programs, DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2409-17490.pdf, PDF pp.2 and 6, section 2 and Appendix A. (11) VLMaterial: Procedural Material Generation with Large Vision-Language Models — fine-tuned VLM emits editable material programs, DBLP_conf_iclr_LiWSZ0BM25.pdf (version alias DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2501-18623.pdf), PDF p.1 and section 4.3. Count aliases once. Explicitly exclude the actual Beyond the Training Distribution paper in DBLP_journals_cacm_AlurSFS18.pdf: it is an empirical generalization study, excluded by the question. Also exclude CRUXEval, LiveCodeBench, Counterfeit Conundrum, the few-shot benchmark, Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet, JoinABLe, the image-sketch component parser, Learning to Acquire Information, Selecting Representative Examples, and control/world-model works. The one-page DBLP_conf_nips_NyeS0L20.pdf is a response letter, not an additional rule-learning paper. Inclusion depends on the implemented method, not a citation to neural synthesis.
input_cases.question: Across the ResearchPapers corpus, enumerate every distinct standalone method or application paper whose own synthesis or repair pipeline trains or fine-tunes a neural model to propose or score executable programs, program fragments, or intermediate program specifications. Include domain-specific applications and hybrid neural-symbolic systems. Exclude benchmark-only or generalization/self-repair studies, recognition without executable program recovery, observation/example selection alone, policy/world-model learning for control, and workflows that only prompt pretrained models without task-specific training. Use actual PDF contents, not filename-implied titles; exclude proceedings, front matter, response letters, and duplicate versions. Give the complete list and explain the neural component's role for each work.

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: enumeration; expected_unique_works: 4. Full gold: (1) Library Learning for Neurally-Guided Bayesian Program Induction (EC2), DBLP_conf_nips_EllisMSST18.pdf — compress step extends the DSL while compile trains recognition, PDF p.1 and section 2. (2) DreamCoder: Growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning, DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2006-08381.pdf — sleep abstraction constructs reusable library routines from waking solutions, PDF p.1 and wake/sleep description. (3) Top-Down Synthesis for Library Learning (Stitch), DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23.pdf — corpus-guided top-down search constructs abstractions that compress existing programs, PDF pp.1–2 and algorithm sections. (4) MathDSL: A Domain-Specific Language for Concise Mathematical Solutions Via Program Synthesis, DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2409-17490.pdf — application of DreamCoder plus Stitch learns reusable equation-solving strategies, PDF pp.2 and 6, section 2 and Appendix A. There are no additional corpus filename aliases for these four. Do not omit MathDSL because it reuses an existing algorithm. Conversely, Synthesizing theories of human language learns cross-language structural biases/metamodels, not a library of new executable DSL abstractions via program compression; SketchAdapt learns sketches rather than extending a reusable library. Fixed primitive collections in SyntRec, SWM and other systems do not qualify simply because they support reuse.
input_cases.question: Across all standalone research papers in ResearchPapers, enumerate every work whose own method learns reusable executable DSL abstractions by compressing or refactoring collections of existing or synthesized programs. Include application papers that actually use such abstraction learning, not only papers introducing a general algorithm. Exclude learning only neural weights or grammar probabilities, fixed hand-written libraries, citations without implementation, proceedings and duplicate versions. For each work describe how learned abstractions are constructed or reused.

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: enumeration; expected_unique_works: 2. Require (1) Automated Feedback Generation for Introductory Programming Assignments, DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1204-1751.pdf — transforms an instructor-supplied error model and reference solution into a constrained repair search and minimizes corrections, PDF p.1 and sections 2.3, 3, 4; (2) sk_p: a neural program corrector for MOOCs, DBLP_conf_oopsla_PuNSB16.pdf, identical alias DBLP_journals_corr_PuNSB16.pdf — trains a seq2seq fragment/statement completion model on correct student programs and searches resulting repairs, PDF p.1 and sections 2, 4. DBLP_conf_pldi_SinghGS13.pdf actually contains Raven: Rethinking Automated Assessment for Scratch Programs via Video-Grounded Evaluation, not the original feedback-generation paper; Raven is excluded because assessment does not generate source corrections. Do not count an arbitrary repair paper just because students could use it.
input_cases.question: Which distinct standalone papers in the entire ResearchPapers corpus automatically generate source-code corrections for students' introductory programming assignments? Enumerate all of them and explain how candidate corrections are obtained. Exclude grading or assessment without code correction, general-purpose LLM repair studies, papers merely citing student repair, proceedings and duplicate versions; use actual PDF contents rather than filename-implied identities.

The Counterfeit Conundrum: Can Code Language Models Grasp the
Nuances of Their Incorrect Generations?
Alex Gu1 Wen-Ding Li⋆2 Naman Jain⋆3 Theo X. Olausson⋆1 Celine Lee⋆2
Koushik Sen3 Armando Solar-Lezama1
1MIT CSAIL 2Cornell University 3University of California, Berkeley
{gua, theoxo}@mit.edu, {wl678, cl923}@cornell.edu, naman_jain@berkeley.edu
Abstract
While language models are increasingly more
proficient at code generation, they still fre-
quently generate incorrect programs. Many of
these programs are obviously wrong, but others
are more subtle and pass weaker correctness
checks such as being able to compile. In this
work, we focus on these counterfeit samples:
programs sampled from a language model that
1) have a high enough log-probability to be gen-
erated at a moderate temperature and 2) pass
weak correctness checks. Overall, we discover
that most models have a very shallow under-
standing of counterfeits through three clear fail-
ure modes. First, models mistakenly classify
them as correct. Second, models are worse
at reasoning about the execution behaviour of
counterfeits and often predict their execution
results as if they were correct. Third, when ask-
ing models to fix counterfeits, the likelihood of
a model successfully repairing a counterfeit is
often even lower than that of sampling a cor-
rect program from scratch. Counterfeits also
have very unexpected properties: first, counter-
feit programs for problems that are easier for
a model to solve are not necessarily easier to
detect and only slightly easier to execute and
repair. Second, counterfeits from a given model
are just as confusing to the model itself as they
are to other models. Finally, both strong and
weak models are able to generate counterfeit
samples that equally challenge all models. In
light of our findings, we recommend that care
and caution be taken when relying on models to
understand their own samples, especially when
no external feedback is incorporated.
1 Introduction
In the past year, language models such as Code
Llama (Roziere et al., 2023), DeepSeek-Coder
(Guo et al., 2024), and GPT-4 (OpenAI, 2023) have
demonstrated great advances in code generation.
Their success has primarily been due to their strong
code generation abilities, as measured by bench-
marks such as HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) and
MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) as well as their use-
fulness in general-purpose code writing. While
these models are able to produce correct code for
impressively complex specifications, they just as
often produce incorrect code.
Some of these incorrect programs contain egre-
gious mistakes, but others fail in more subtle ways.
We focus our attention towards the second group,
which we call counterfeit samples. We define a
counterfeit sample to be a program sampled from a
code language model which is 1) good enough to
be generated by the language model at a moderate
temperature and 2) pass weak but nontrivial cor-
rectness checks. In this work, we study the extent
to which models can understand these counterfeit
programs. The second criterion of passing nontriv-
ial correctness checks distinguishes programs with
more subtle errors from those that trivially fail and
are likely uninteresting. In Fig. 1, we show an
example of an incorrect, counterfeit, and correct
program. Because we use relatively weak correct-
ness checks, many counterfeit programs can still
be easily detected as wrong by a human.
We provide empirical evidence that code lan-
guage models have a shallow understanding of
these counterfeit samples (Sec. 3) via three evalua-
tions: correctness checking, execution prediction,
and program repair. For correctness checking, the
model is asked to assess whether a short piece of
code correctly implements a natural language spec-
ification (sometimes with test cases). For execution
prediction, the model is given a program-input pair
and asked to predict the output of executing the pro-
gram on the given input. For fairness, we ensure
the programs are generally short and that execution
does not require complex calculations. For repair,
the model is given the counterfeit program along-
side its original specification and is asked to correct
it. First, we find that models frequently misjudge

of weaker models, as stronger models are less likely to generate obvious mistakes. In Fig. 9, we

(DS-33B, CL-34B) and weaker (CL-7B, SC) models. Note that this is the same as Fig. 8 with each
row aggregated and filtered to only include counterfeit samples. Since there does not seem to be
a significant difference between the difficulties, models of all strengths can be used to generate
counterfeit samples that are challenging for models to understand.

Figure 9: Accuracy of correctness and execution tasks on counterfeit samples. Both strong and
weak models are able to generate difficult counterfeit samples.
5 Qualitative Analysis
In general, most counterfeit programs fall into one of three broad categories: (1) error in algorithmic
design or implementation, (2) incorrectly understanding or completely ignoring details in the
specification, (3) failing to address corner cases in the input space. Examples of each are provided
in Appendix E.
5.1 Failure Modes on Correctness Checking
In Sec. 3, we saw that GPT-4 is significantly more performant than other models at both correctness
checking and execution prediction. Yet, we still find a significant fraction of failures. In this section,
we take a closer look at the performance of GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 to understand where today’s
cutting-edge models still fall short. Through a manual inspection of examples, we uncover three
main failure modes for verifying the correctness of counterfeit samples. Here, we present one
example of each, deferring more to Appendix F. For conciseness and readability, some of the
problem statements have been altered from their original form.
1) The model does not catch misunderstood or ignored details in the specification : Sometimes,
the verification model doesn’t catch important specification details that are misunderstood or
ignored by the counterfeit sample.

5 Qualitative Analysis
In general, most counterfeit programs fall into one
of three broad categories: (1) error in algorithmic
design or implementation, (2) incorrectly under-
standing or completely ignoring details in the spec-
ification, (3) failing to address corner cases in the
input space. Examples of each are provided in
Appendix E.
5.1 Failure Modes on Correctness Checking

cutting-edge models still fall short. Through a man-

failure modes for verifying the correctness of coun-

1 Introduction
In the past year, language models such as CodeLlama (Roziere et al., 2023), DeepSeek-Coder (Guo
et al., 2024), and GPT-4 (OpenAI, 2023) have demonstrated great advances in code generation.
Their success has primarily been due to their strong code generation abilities, as measured by
benchmarks such as HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) as well as their
usefulness in general-purpose code writing. While these models are able to produce correct code
for impressively complex specifications, they just as often produce incorrect code.
Some of these incorrect programs contain egregious mistakes, but others fail in more subtle ways.
We focus our attention towards the second group, which we call counterfeit samples. We define
a counterfeit sample to be a program sampled from a code language model which is 1) good
enough to be generated by the language model at a moderate temperature, 2) are incorrect, and 3)
pass weak but nontrivial correctness checks. In this work, we study the extent to which models
can understand these counterfeit programs. This final criterion of passing nontrivial correctness
checks distinguishes programs with more subtle errors from those that trivially fail and are likely
uninteresting. In Fig. 1, we show an example of an incorrect, counterfeit, and correct program.
Because we use relatively weak correctness checks, many counterfeit programs can still be easily
detected as wrong by a human.
Given a list of distinct strings, check if any two have the same length. 
>>> same_length([“aa”, “b”, “ccc”, “dd”]) 
True
>>> same_length([“a”, “bb”, “ccc”]) 
False
Correct
def same_length(s): 
   l = [len(i) for i in s] 
   l = set(l) 
   if len(s) > len(l): 
       return True 
   return False 
Counterfeit
def same_length(s): 
   if s == []: return False 
   for a, b in zip(s, s): 
       if len(a) == len(b): 
           return True 
   return False 
Incorrect
def same_length(s): 
   # check the length of s. 
   if len(s) == 7: 
       return s * s 
   else: 
       return s + s 
Figure 1: Example of a problem specification with incorrect, counterfeit, and correct programs.
We provide empirical evidence that code language models have a shallow understanding of these
counterfeit samples (Sec. 3) via three evaluations: correctness checking, execution prediction, and
program repair. For correctness checking, the model is asked to assess whether a short piece
of code correctly implements a natural language specification (sometimes with test cases). For
execution prediction, the model is given a program-input pair and asked to predict the output
of executing the program on the given input. For fairness, we ensure the programs are generally
short and that execution does not require complex calculations. For repair, the model is given the
counterfeit program alongside its original specification and is asked to correct it. First, we find
that models frequently misjudge counterfeit samples as correct. Second, models are much worse
at reasoning about the execution of counterfeits than their correct companions, often executing
counterfeits as if their semantics matched those of a correct program. Third, models falter at repair:
the likelihood of a model successfully repairing a counterfeit example is often even lower than that
of generating a correct program when sampling from scratch. As a caveat, this paper focuses on
open-source models, primarily CodeLlama 34B and DeepSeek Instruct 33B. We also present limited
results on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 which suggest that GPT-3.5 behaves similarly to the open-source

models while GPT-4 has a much better understanding of counterfeits. Nevertheless, we still find
that GPT-4 still exhibits some of these misunderstandings.
Through further analysis, we find that counterfeit samples have other unexpected properties (Sec.
4). We find, for example, that counterfeit samples from problems that are easier for the model
to solve are not easier to assess and only slightly easier to execute and repair, highlighting an
inconsistency between generation and understanding capabilities. We also observe that models
don’t perceive their own counterfeit samples differently from other models’ counterfeits and that
models of all capability levels are able to generate equally difficult counterfeit samples.
Overall, we find that these counterfeit samples are, in a sense, adversarial to the model: models
often struggle to assess their correctness, reason about their execution as if they were correct
programs, and repair them at a low rate. Understanding counterfeit samples is a prerequisite to
many downstream applications in which models use their own feedback to improve themselves.
Therefore, in light of our findings, we recommend exercising caution in these schemes such
as self-repair and model-based reranking of outputs, especially when no external feedback is
incorporated.
2 Experimental Setup
2.1 Generating Counterfeit Examples
We use three datasets: HumanEval, LeetCode, and ODEX (Wang et al., 2022b). HumanEval
evaluates code generation of simple natural language descriptions, LeetCode is a harder dataset
of the same flavor using programming interview practice problems, and ODEX tests knowledge
of diverse Python libraries. To generate counterfeit examples, we first sample programs from
CodeLlama (CL), DeepSeek-Coder Instruct (DS-I), and StarCoder (SC) at temperature T = 0.6.
Of the incorrect programs, we design a dataset-specific filter to remove incorrect programs that
do not pass mild correctness criteria. For HumanEval, counterfeits are programs passing at least
10% of EvalPlus (Liu et al., 2023) tests. For LeetCode, counterfeits are programs that received a
“Wrong Answer” verdict, which filters out programs that crashed during runtime or took too long
to finish. For ODEX, counterfeits are programs that can be successfully parsed by ast.parse and
are under 500 characters. In Fig. 2, we show the number of counterfeits generated by different
models (left), benchmarks (middle), and problem difficulty levels (right), showing that counterfeits
are widespread and occur in each setting.
2.2 Code Understanding Tasks
We evaluate counterfeits on the following tasks:
Correctness Checking: The goal is to check whether a model-generated Python program (either correct
or counterfeit) correctly implements a natural language (NL) specification. These specifications
often include input-output examples. We use CoT with majority voting (Wei et al., 2022; Wang
et al., 2022a) and report accuracy.
Execution Prediction: The goal is to predict the execution output of a given model-generated Python
program on a specific input. We use an execution-based metric for correctness and report pass@1,
the fraction of samples that are correct.

(Olausson et al., 2024); as such, self-repair may
give us further insight into the model’s capabilities.

Studies like (Schneider et al., 2023; Matelsky et al., 2023) investigate LLMs as auto-graders or judges
for educators. On the other hand, Valmeekam et al. (2023); Tyen et al. (2023); Stechly et al. (2023);
Chen et al. (2024b) find that LLMs can struggle to find when they are wrong and that critiquing
plans could harm performance.
Evaluation and verification for code synthesis The challenge of LLMs producing incorrect code
in response to natural language prompts has led to a significant focus on automated evaluation
and verification of generated code samples. Various studies have demonstrated that postprocessing
the samples from LLMs can substantially enhance the accuracy of the system (Chen et al., 2022;
Ridnik et al., 2024; Key et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023b; Li et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2023a).
Also, Inala et al. (2022); Zhang et al. (2023d); Ni et al. (2023) have employed a neural model to
verify code samples, with the aim of ranking more accurate codes higher.
Code understanding in language models Many benchmarks evaluate aspects of code understand-
ing and code intelligence such as code summarization (Iyer et al., 2016; Hasan et al., 2021), commit
message generation (Liu et al., 2020), code comprehension (Singhal et al., 2024), clone detection (Lu
et al., 2021), code question answering (Sahu et al., 2022), and code explaining (Muennighoff et al.,
2023). Neural-based code execution has been studied in (Austin et al., 2021; Nye et al., 2021; Gu
et al., 2024; La Malfa et al., 2024), and code repair has been studied in (Madaan et al., 2023; Chen
et al., 2024a; Zhang et al., 2023a; Olausson et al., 2024), and Liu et al. (2024) examine a suite of code
reasoning benchmarks.
A few controlled studies highlight the extent to which language models understand code. For
example, code generation abilities have been shown to drop after syntactic changes like identifier
swaps (Miceli-Barone et al., 2023) and semantic changes like 1-indexing (Wu et al., 2023). Dinh
et al. (2024) show that models fail at completing code with bugs. Jin and Rinard (2023) provide
evidence that LMs can learn meaningful representations when trained on programs, Zhang et al.
(2023c) explore the behavior of transformers to simulate recursive functions, and Min et al. (2023)
discover that code language models are inconsistent on various coding tasks.
Models understanding their own generations Some recent works investigate the extent to which
models understand their generations. Huang et al. (2023b); Chen et al. (2024a); Tyen et al. (2023);
Olausson et al. (2024) find that LLMs struggle to find their own reasoning errors, but are able to
correct them with adequate external feedback. Singhal et al. (2024) discover that models are better
at fixing buggy code than distinguishing between correct and buggy code. Relevant to our work,
West et al. (2023) and Oh et al. (2024) argue that generative capability may not be contingent on
understanding capability in textual domains.
7 Conclusion
In this work, we bring attention to the counterfeit samples of a code language model: incorrect
programs that a model thinks are correct and can pass surface-level correctness checks. We observe
that in a sense, these counterfeit samples are adversarial to the model: models often cannot assess
their correctness, reason about their execution, and struggle to repair them. Compared to other

syntax, documentation about the API, clues about the algori thm to be written, or examples of
similar functionality being written. Ding et al. (2023) ﬁnd that even when the oracle context is re-

Example: Bad Generation Despite Identifying the Correct Co ntext: Ding et al. (2023) high-
lights a failure case where a code LLM fails to complete a Pyth on test case cor-
rectly , even though it has the correct context. The function name from the context,
test case convert camel to snake, suggests that the function being completed is a test
case for convert camel to snake. With the given context, the model generates the function
as convert camel to snake, which however does not match the larger codebase as other
pieces of code expect this function name to be camel to snake. While this issue can partly
be attributed to incomplete retrieval of relevant informat ion, it also presents a challenge for
code LLMs, as they must recognize such inconsistencies—esp ecially when the immediate
context is correctly provided—thereby avoiding high-conﬁ dence errors.
3.6 Semantic Understanding of Codebases
Being able to effectively write code relies on having a stron g semantic understanding
(somewhat like a world model) of the entire codebase: struct urally seeing how various
parts of the code go together, knowing what is implemented wh ere, understanding how
the algorithms work, and keeping track of program invariant s at certain program points.
LLMs struggle with this global semantic understanding
Potential solutions: 4.1
A global and holistic semantic understanding of a codebase i s important for performing almost
all code-related tasks. For example, let’s say an engineer i s asked to improve the runtime perfor-
mance of a query . T o do so, they must ﬁrst understand the codeb ase’s structure well enough to
know where all the pieces of the algorithm are implemented. T hen, they need to understand the
algorithm and implementation in detail. This includes both the high-level algorithm (including
its time complexity) and the low-level implementation deta ils to identify both algorithmic and
implementation bottlenecks. Finally , after coming up with a solution, they must then return to
their understanding of the global code structure so that the y can integrate their new algorithm
without introducing new bugs.
LLMs struggle at semantic understanding of codebases for se veral reasons. First, the way that code
is pieced together can be relatively intricate, and underst anding all these complex relationships
can be difﬁcult. Second, code can often have units with high l ogical complexity that contain
custom algorithms that may never have appeared anywhere in t he training data. Finally , because
a disproportionately large number of LLM training tokens ar e spent on code generation rather
than other coding tasks, models may lack a holistic awarenes s and world model of code.
One desiderata is that models can generalize knowledge acro ss various coding tasks
(Roychoudhury and Zeller , 2025). However, this may not be straightforward as just training on
more tasks: Gu et al. (2024) found that coding models ﬁne-tuned on additional natural l anguage/-
code pairs saw signiﬁcant improvements on code generation b ut did not transfer to improving

Generations?

MIT CSAIL
Abstract
While language models are increasingly more proficient at code generation, they still
frequently generate incorrect programs. Many of these programs are obviously wrong,
but others are more subtle and pass weaker correctness checks such as being able to
compile. In this work, we focus on these counterfeit samples: programs sampled from
a language model that 1) have a high enough log-probability to be generated at a
moderate temperature and 2) pass weak correctness checks. Overall, we discover that
most models have a very shallow understanding of counterfeits through three clear
failure modes. First, models mistakenly classify them as correct. Second, models are
worse at reasoning about the execution behaviour of counterfeits and often predict their
execution results as if they were correct. Third, when asking models to fix counterfeits,
the likelihood of a model successfully repairing a counterfeit is often even lower than
that of sampling a correct program from scratch. Counterfeits also have very unexpected
properties: first, counterfeit programs for problems that are easier for a model to solve
are not necessarily easier to detect and only slightly easier to execute and repair. Second,
counterfeits from a given model are just as confusing to the model itself as they are to
other models. Finally, both strong and weak models are able to generate counterfeit
samples that equally challenge all models. In light of our findings, we recommend that
care and caution be taken when relying on models to understand their own samples,
especially when no external feedback is incorporated.

et al. 2017], which operates on (numeric) symbolic terms constrained by an SMT formula (e.g.:
linear arithmetic). We are interested in future work combining these techniques to automatically
derive more-precise analyses.
In §6, we explained how abstract rewriting is similar to narrowing, but different in an important
way. There is a long tradition in narrowing of proving lifting lemmas similar to our own; the first
comes from Hullot [1980].
In App. E, we discuss the use of several terms similar to “abstract matching” in the contexts of
abstract interpretation of logic programs, model-checking, and term-rewriting engines, as well as
several minor uses of syntactic abstraction.
Control-Flow Analysis. Many papers have been written on control-flow analysis [Jagannathan and
Weeks 1995; Jones 1981; Midtgaard 2012; Shivers 1991]. Older research tries to manually construct
a complicated analysis of programs with highly-dynamic control flow. Our work automatically
constructs CFG-generators from first principles. Our goal is not to analyze complex programs, but
to match the work of hand-written CFG-generators with minimal user input.
As such, we do not consider this work as part of the literature on control-flow analysis. Owing to
their different emphasis, these works uniformly have three limitations that make them unsuitable
for automatically deriving CFG-generators:
(1) While they explain how a human could define a new analysis for different languages, their
analyses are ultimately manually defined for each language. They further repeat this manual
construction for every abstraction used.
(2) They check that their result safely approximates executions, but pay no attention to the shape
of the graph.
(3) Most importantly, they manually partition program states into equivalence classes. That is, they
manually annotate the program with labels or program-points, using these as CFG nodes. This
is a hindrance to both automation and theory, as most type theories do not contain labels. A
major motivation of this work is to support our ongoing work on combining analyses with
different notions of program point (i.e.: partition program states differently), which makes not
hardcoding them especially important.
App. E gives a brief overview of control-flow analysis, and discusses two works that deserve special
mention, due to use of abstract machines and focus on generality.
9 CONCLUSION
This work presented both an algorithm for constructing CFGs from first principles and the world’s
first CFG-generator generator. Yet our work also furthers three larger goals.
First, we have provided an answer to “what is a control-flow graph?” beyond the vague “a CFG is
an abstraction of control-flow:” A CFG is a projection of the transition graph of abstracted abstract
machine states. This fulfills our original impetus for this work, that of needing to create static
analyzers with exotic notions of “program point. ”
Second, we have introduced abstract rewriting as a simple yet powerful technique for deriving
tools from a language’s semantics. We are excited by the idea of using it to derive other artifacts
from language semantics, such as a symbol-table generator from the typing abstract-machine
[Sergey and Clarke 2011].
Third, we have used a language’s semantics to derive a tool entirely unlike a semantics. Though
it’s long been known that a semantics can be executed to obtain an interpreter or even a symbolic-

models while GPT-4 has a much better understanding of counterfeits. Nevertheless, we still find
that GPT-4 still exhibits some of these misunderstandings.
Through further analysis, we find that counterfeit samples have other unexpected properties (Sec.
4). We find, for example, that counterfeit samples from problems that are easier for the model
to solve are not easier to assess and only slightly easier to execute and repair, highlighting an
inconsistency between generation and understanding capabilities. We also observe that models
don’t perceive their own counterfeit samples differently from other models’ counterfeits and that
models of all capability levels are able to generate equally difficult counterfeit samples.
Overall, we find that these counterfeit samples are, in a sense, adversarial to the model: models
often struggle to assess their correctness, reason about their execution as if they were correct
programs, and repair them at a low rate. Understanding counterfeit samples is a prerequisite to
many downstream applications in which models use their own feedback to improve themselves.
Therefore, in light of our findings, we recommend exercising caution in these schemes such
as self-repair and model-based reranking of outputs, especially when no external feedback is
incorporated.
2 Experimental Setup
2.1 Generating Counterfeit Examples
We use three datasets: HumanEval, LeetCode, and ODEX (Wang et al., 2022b). HumanEval
evaluates code generation of simple natural language descriptions, LeetCode is a harder dataset
of the same flavor using programming interview practice problems, and ODEX tests knowledge
of diverse Python libraries. To generate counterfeit examples, we first sample programs from
CodeLlama (CL), DeepSeek-Coder Instruct (DS-I), and StarCoder (SC) at temperature T = 0.6.
Of the incorrect programs, we design a dataset-specific filter to remove incorrect programs that
do not pass mild correctness criteria. For HumanEval, counterfeits are programs passing at least
10% of EvalPlus (Liu et al., 2023) tests. For LeetCode, counterfeits are programs that received a
“Wrong Answer” verdict, which filters out programs that crashed during runtime or took too long
to finish. For ODEX, counterfeits are programs that can be successfully parsed by ast.parse and
are under 500 characters. In Fig. 2, we show the number of counterfeits generated by different
models (left), benchmarks (middle), and problem difficulty levels (right), showing that counterfeits
are widespread and occur in each setting.
2.2 Code Understanding Tasks
We evaluate counterfeits on the following tasks:
Correctness Checking: The goal is to check whether a model-generated Python program (either correct
or counterfeit) correctly implements a natural language (NL) specification. These specifications
often include input-output examples. We use CoT with majority voting (Wei et al., 2022; Wang
et al., 2022a) and report accuracy.
Execution Prediction: The goal is to predict the execution output of a given model-generated Python
program on a specific input. We use an execution-based metric for correctness and report pass@1,
the fraction of samples that are correct.

The older work by Hannan and Miller [1992] is very limited. They give a few examples of

The Sketching Approach to Program Synthesis
Armando Solar-Lezama
Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract. Sketching is a new form of localized software synthesis that
aims to bridge the gap between a programmer’s high-level insights about
a problem and the computer’s ability to manage low-level details. In
sketching, the programmer uses partial programs to describe the desired
implementation strategy, and leaves the low-level details of the imple-
mentation to an automated synthesis procedure. This paper describes
the sketching approach to program synthesis, including the details of the
Sketch language and synthesizer. The paper will then describe some of
the techniques that make synthesis from sketches possible, and will close
with a brief discussion of open problems in programmer guided synthesis.
1 Introduction
Sketching is a new form of localized program synthesis that allows programmers
to express their high-level insights about a problem by writing asketch—a partial
program that encodes the structure of a solution while leaving its low-level details
unspeciﬁed. In addition to the sketch, programmers provide the synthesizer with
either a reference implementation or a set of test routines that the synthesized
code must pass. TheSketch synthesis engine is able to derive the missing details
in the sketch to produce a working implementation that satisﬁes the correctness
criteria established by the programmer. By combining the programmers insight
expressed in the sketch with the synthesizer’s ability to reason exhaustively about
all the low-level details of the problem, sketching allows complex algorithms to
be implemented with minimal human eﬀort.
To illustrate the use of sketching on an interesting programming problem,
consider the problem of reversing a linked list. It is relatively easy to write a
recursive solution to this problem, but the performance of the simple implemen-
tation is likely to be unacceptable. A more eﬃcient implementation must use a
loop instead of recursion, and must construct the new list backwards to avoid
the linear storage. Sketching allows the programmer to express these insights as
a partial program without having to think too much about the details of the
implementation.
The sketch for this problem is shown in Figure 1. The body of reverseEﬃcient
encodes the basic structure of the solution: allocate a new list, and perform a
series of conditional pointer assignments inside a while loop. In order to deﬁne the
space of possible conditionals and assignments, the sketch uses regular expression
notation to deﬁne sets of expressions in lines 1 to 3. The sketch, in short, encodes

3 Problem Overview
In order to describe the details of our approach, we ﬁrst describe a few key
features of theSketch synthesis system which will serve both as a component
and as a target forSw apper. Sketch is an open source system for synthesis
from partial programs. A partial program (also called a sketch) is a program with
holes, where the potential code to complete the holes is drawn from a ﬁnite set
of candidates, often deﬁned as a set of expressions or a grammar. Given a partial
program with a set of assertions, theSketch synthesizer ﬁnds a completion for
the holes that satisﬁes the assertions for all inputs from a given input space.
Sketch uses symbolic execution to derive a predicateP (x,c ) that encodes
the requirement that given a choicec for how to complete the program, the pro-

where equivalent nodes have been collapsed into a single node by structural
hashing [26]. The grammar for this language of expressions is shown in Fig. 1.
The formula simpliﬁcation pass that is the subject of this paper is applied to
this predicateP (x,c ) as it is constructed and before the predicate is solved in an
abstraction reﬁnement loop based on counterexample guided inductive synthesis
(CEGIS).

Mocks from Tests
Nate F. F. Bragg1, Jerey S. Foster 1, Cody Roux 2,
1 Tufts University, Medford, MA 02155, USA

Abstract. Sketch is a popular program synthesis tool that solves for
unknowns in a sketch or partial program. However, while Sketch is pow-
erful, it does not directly support modular synthesis of dependencies,
potentially limiting scalability. In this paper, we introduce Sketcham,
a new technique that modularizes a regular sketch by automatically
generating mocks|functions that approximate the behavior of complete
implementations|from the sketch’s test suite. For example, if the func-
tionf originally calls g, Sketcham creates a mock gm fromg’s tests and
augments the sketch with a version off that callsgm. This change allows
the unknowns in f andg to be solved separately, enabling modular syn-
thesis with no extra work from the Sketch user. We evaluated Sketcham
on ten benchmarks, performing enough runs to show at a 95% con dence
level that Sketcham improves median synthesis performance on six of our
ten benchmarks by a factor of up to 5  compared to plain Sketch, in-
cluding one benchmark that times out on Sketch, while exhibiting similar
performance on the remaining four. Our results show that Sketcham can
achieve modular synthesis by automatically generating mocks from tests.
Keywords: Program synthesis, mocks, Sketch
1 Introduction
Program synthesis by sketching, as embodied by the Sketch synthesis tool [30],
is a popular technique that has been applied to a wide variety of problems
[5,7,13,14,15,16,18,22,29]. A Sketch input (henceforth a sketch) is a program
written in a C-like language augmented with holes, unknown constants, and gen-
erators, unknown expressions. The solution for a sketch is speci ed using test
cases called harnesses, also written in the Sketch language, that make assertions
about the results of to-be-synthesized code. Sketch searches for a solution using
counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS) , which alternately synthe-
sizes a candidate solution and then uses a veri er to check the assertions; any
counterexamples from veri cation feed into the next round of synthesis [27].

Jinseong Jeon† Xiaokang Qiu‡ Jeffrey S. Foster† Armando Solar-Lezama‡

Abstract
Sketch-based synthesis, epitomized by the S KETCH tool, lets de-
velopers synthesize software starting from a partial program, also
called a sketch or template. This paper presents JS KETCH , a tool
that brings sketch-based synthesis to Java. JS KETCH ’s input is a
partial Java program that may include holes, which are unknown
constants, expression generators, which range over sets of expres-
sions, and class generators, which are partial classes. JS KETCH
then translates the synthesis problem into a S KETCH problem; this
translation is complex because S KETCH is not object-oriented. Fi-
nally, JS KETCH synthesizes an executable Java program by inter-
preting the output of SKETCH .
Categories and Subject Descriptors I.2.2 [Automatic Program-
ming]: Program Synthesis; F.3.1 [ Specifying and Verifying and
Reasoning about Programs]: Assertions, Speciﬁcation techniques
General Terms Design, Languages.
Keywords Program Synthesis, Programming by Example, Java,
SKETCH , Input-output Examples.
1. Introduction
Program synthesis [5, 6] is an attractive programming paradigm
that aims to automate the development of complex pieces of code.
Deriving programs completely from scratch given only a declar-
ative speciﬁcation is very challenging for all but the simplest al-
gorithms, but recent work has shown that the problem can be made
tractable by starting from a partial program—referred to in the liter-
ature as a sketch [11], scaffold [13] or template—that constrains the
space of possible programs the synthesizer needs to consider. This
approach to synthesis has proven useful in a variety of domains
including program inversion [14], program deobfuscation [4], de-
velopment of concurrent data-structures [12] and even automated
tutoring [8].
This paper presents JS KETCH , a tool that makes sketch-based
synthesis directly available to Java programmers. JSKETCH is built
as a frontend on top of the SKETCH synthesis system, a mature syn-
thesis tool based on a simple imperative language that can generate
C code [11]. JS KETCH allows Java programmers to use many of
the S KETCH ’s synthesis features, such as the ability to write code
with unknown constants ( holes written ??) and unknown expres-
sions described by a generator (written{| e∗|}). In addition, JS-
KETCH provides a new synthesis feature—a class-level generator—
that is speciﬁcally tailored for object oriented programs. Section 2
walks through JS KETCH ’s input and output, along with a running
example.
As illustrated in Figure 1, JS KETCH compiles a Java pro-
gram with unknowns to a partial program in the S KETCH lan-
guage and then maps the result of S KETCH synthesis back to
Java. The translation to S KETCH is challenging because S KETCH
is not object oriented, so the translator must model the com-
plex object-oriented features in Java—such as inheritance, method

Program Synthesis with models. As discussed earlier, our work builds on
work by Singh et al. [24], who propose manually created models for Sketch.
While Sketcham relies on the core algorithm of that work, Sketcham frees the
Sketch user from needing to write models, because we create mocks automat-
ically from normal sketches. Mariano et al. [18] use algebraic speci cations to
model libraries. In contrast, our approach derives speci cations from the input
program’s assertions, without requiring the programmer to add annotations.
Deriving mocks and specs from tests. Sa et al. [21] use the capture and re-
play of actual test executions to automatically generate mock dependencies with
the goal of speeding up test execution. Fazzini et al. [8] further generalize this
capture-and-replay technique to consistently model the environment of a mo-
bile app under test, allowing for testing apps that use an inconsistent resource
like a database or network device. Both of these target normal testing rather
than synthesis. Nguyen et al. [19] leverage symbolic execution over input-output
test pairs to perform program repair. However, they use these tests to model
individual expressions instead of modeling entire functions. The insight under-
lying these approaches is similar to ours, however Sketcham is capable of both
input-output pairs and general properties, and does not rely on either concrete
or symbolic execution of tests.
Component-based synthesis. Gulwani et al. [10] model programs using logical
input-output relations to synthesize loop-free bit-vector programs. Shi et al. [23]
combine many solutions that each only partially meet a speci cation into one
that meets the entire speci cation. Both approaches limit the synthesis search
space by building their solutions from the bottom up, from a selection of base
components. Smith and Albarghouthi [25] prune the search space using bottom
up algebraic rewriting of the program into an equivalent normal form. In contrast
to these, Sketcham derives its bene ts from breaking apart input sketches from
the top down, at function level granularity.
Modular synthesis using symbolic or actual execution. Samak et al. [22] de-
rive speci cations of class methods using symbolic execution and use them to
synthesize a replacement shim class one method at a time. Van Geen et al. [31]
use symbolic execution to model abstract virtual machines to modularly syn-
thesize a compiler one instruction at a time. In contrast, because our approach
derives mocks directly from the input’s assertions, we need not consider the code
itself when modeling it. Hua et al. [11] modularize the synthesis of library calls
through execution of actual partial programs. In contrast, we attempt to avoid
called functions entirely by relying on their inferred speci cations.
Other approaches. Bod k et al. [2]  nalize incomplete programs using angelic
nondeterminism. In contrast, Sketcham does not introduce arbitrary angelic val-
ues, but instead constrains any angelic-like behavior using a function’s inferred
speci cation. Huang et al. [12] use a divide-and-conquer strategy to iteratively
split synthesis problems according to heuristics. In contrast, Sketcham splits
problems structurally in a single pass. Polikarpova et al. [20] speed up synthesis
through modular veri cation using re nement types. In contrast, our approach
achieves a similar kind of modularity without being type-directed.
